description_full: Service Corporation International provides deathcare products and services in the United States and Canada. Its funeral service and cemetery operations comprise funeral service locations, cemeteries, funeral service/cemetery combination locations, crematoria, and other businesses. The company also provides professional services related to funerals and cremations, including the use of funeral home facilities and motor vehicles, arranging and directing services, removal, preparation, embalming, cremation, memorialization, and travel protection, as well as catering services. In addition, it offers funeral merchandise, including burial caskets and related accessories, urns and other cremation receptacles, outer burial containers, flowers, online and video tributes, stationery products, casket and cremation memorialization products, and other ancillary merchandise. Further, the company's cemeteries provide cemetery property interment rights, such as developed lots, lawn crypts, mausoleum spaces, and cremation niches; custom inventory, including private mausoleums, family estates, and exclusive cremation memorialization options; and Cemetery merchandise and services, such as memorial cemetery markers and bases, outer burial containers, flowers and floral placement, other ancillary merchandise, graveside services, merchandise installation, and interments. It offers its products and services under the Dignity Memorial, Dignity Planning, National Cremation Society, Advantage Funeral and Cremation Services, Funeraria del Angel, Making Everlasting Memories, Neptune Society, and Trident Society brand names. Service Corporation International was incorporated in 1962 and is headquartered in Houston, Texas.

financial_summary: Service Corporation Internation is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $10.2B market cap on $4.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 12% against a 7% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, and 24% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $554M in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.74× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.1× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 3.8×.

Management returns a meaningful 6.3% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 3.0% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 2.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 18% below the high.

val: The stock trades 22% below its DCF fair value of $96.00, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 29%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $69.86 to $135 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 38% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.4% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.4% (vs the 8% bar).

The price implies 2.2% annual cash-flow growth, 5pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 12% earns above the cost of capital of 7.0%, but the 5pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.31).
It runs a 24% gross margin and converts 13% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.74x.
ROE of 33% is amplified by 11.4x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.4% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.1x net debt to EBITDA ($243.6M of cash against $5.2B of debt), with interest covered 3.8x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.78 in the distress zone.
The current ratio of 0.55 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.6% over 3 years and 3.7% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 25% of profits supports about 3.0% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Capex runs 1.8x depreciation (9.0% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Analysts expect 8.3% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 3.0%, and institutions hold 97%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (5 sales, net $29.0M sold).
It returns 6.3% a year to shareholders (4.5% in buybacks and 1.9% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 3.6% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 21 consecutive years, raising it 6.0% a year over the last five.
people: With about 25,000 employees, each generates about $172K of revenue, 0.5x the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 4.6% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $22K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.8M (28x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
